 He Can Make His 2026 IRA Contribution All the Way Until Tax Day in April 2027. Most People Think the Window Closes December 31
 David Beren Tue, November 3, 2026 at 3:13 PM EST 6 min read Quick Read 
 The IRA contribution deadline for 2026 is April 15, 2027, not December 31, giving savers several extra months after year-end. 
 The 2026 IRA contribution limit rose to $7,500, or $8,600 for those 50 and older, up from $7,000 and $8,000 in 2025. 
 Roth conversions, RMDs, and qualified charitable distributions still must be completed by December 31 and don't get the April extension. 
 Read More: Avoid these 13 retirement mistakes before they derail your future (sponsor) 
 Savers who skipped an IRA contribution this year might assume the window shuts on December 31. Under IRS rules, the IRA contribution deadline for 2026 falls on the tax filing date in April 2027. That leaves several months after the year ends to contribute to a traditional or Roth IRA and still count it toward 2026. 
 24/7 Wall St. How the April Deadline Works 
 The rule links the contribution deadline to the tax return due date for the year. IRS Publication 590-A says contributions can be made during the year "or by the due date for filing your return for that year, not including extensions." 
 Roth IRAs follow the same schedule, and the IRS says most people could make 2025 Roth contributions until April 15, 2026. Under federal law, individual returns are due on the 15th day of April following the close of the calendar year, which sets the deadline for 2026 contributions at April 15, 2027. If a tax deadline lands on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, it moves to the next business day. 
 Where the Rule Lives in the Tax Code 
 The statute is 26 U.S.C. § 219(f)(3). It treats a contribution as made on the last day of the prior tax year if it's made "on account of such taxable year" and no later than the return due date "not including extensions thereof." Health savings accounts follow that same rule through § 223(d)(4)(B), so 2026 HSA contributions run on the same April timeline.

 The 2026 HSA limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage. For a 401(k), employee deferrals come out of paychecks, and they generally must be made by December 31 of the plan year. 
 Story Continues Who Can Use It and Who Gets Shut Out 
 Contributing requires taxable compensation, which the IRS sums up as "what you earn from working." That covers wages, tips, bonuses, commissions, and self-employment income. On a joint return, one spouse's compensation can support contributions to spouses' separate IRAs, subject to the annual limits and their combined taxable compensation. Roth eligibility also depends on modified adjusted gross income (MAGI), which is adjusted gross income with a few add-backs. 
 For 2026, the Roth limit starts shrinking for single filers at $153,000 and disappears at $168,000. For joint filers, the range runs from $242,000 to $252,000. Married people filing separately who lived together during the year lose Roth eligibility at $10,000 of MAGI. 
 What the Extra Months Allow 
 Some savers wait for the full-year numbers. Once you know your 2026 income, choosing between traditional and Roth gets easier. For workers covered by a workplace plan, the traditional IRA deduction phase-out is between $81,000 and $91,000 for single filers. For married couples filing jointly, the range is $129,000 to $149,000 when one spouse is covered by a workplace plan. If the IRA contributor is not covered by a workplace plan but their spouse is, the deduction phases out between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers. 
 Contribution caps rose for 2026. The 2026 IRA limit is $7,500, or $8,600 for people 50 or older, up from $7,000 and $8,000 in 2025. Traditional contributions reduce the room left for Roth contributions, so the cap covers all IRAs combined. 
 A tax refund can help fund the contribution. The IRS allows people to file a return claiming a traditional IRA contribution before making the contribution, as long as the money goes in by the deadline. An early refund can fund the deposit. 
 Custodians need to know the contribution year. For money deposited between January 1 and April 15, tell the custodian it's for 2026. 
 Traps That Can Trigger a 6% Penalty 
 Labeling matters because if the custodian isn't told which year a contribution covers, it may assume and report to the IRS that the contribution is for the current year. Excess contributions face a 6% excise tax under 26 U.S.C. § 4973 for each year they stay in the account. If income ends up too high for a Roth, you can withdraw the excess contribution and its related earnings by the tax return due date, including extensions. The contribution is then treated as if it were never made, while the earnings remain taxable. 
 Year-End Moves That Still Need December 31 
 Several other IRA moves still run on a calendar-year basis. Traditional IRA distributions are taxable in the year you receive them, and Roth conversions follow that rule, so a conversion meant for 2026 has to happen in 2026. Required minimum distributions (RMDs) for any year after the first one must be made by December 31. 
 A qualified charitable distribution (QCD) sends IRA money straight to a charity and counts toward the required minimum distribution, so a QCD meant to cover the 2026 RMD must also go out before year-end. For the 2026 IRA or HSA contribution itself, the deadline is April 15, 2027.
